title: Piezoelectric resonators in thin-film barium titanate from room temperature to millikelvin
authors: Hao Tian, Shu-Yuan Chang, Nuha Akhtar, Kasra Sardashti, Mohammad Mirhosseini
abstract: Ferroelectric materials, with their strong nonlinearities, underpin key technologies across radio-frequency (RF) signal processing, optical communications, and emerging quantum systems. Barium titanate (BTO) is a notable example, combining strong piezoelectric and electro-optic responses. While bulk BTO has been studied for decades, the piezoelectric properties of its recently available thin films, and their behavior at the millikelvin temperatures relevant to quantum hardware, remain largely unexplored. Here, we fabricate and characterize surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators on thin-film BTO. The measured devices exhibit high electromechanical coupling (k2eff 0.14 at 5.2 GHz) and operate up to 7.8 GHz. From these measurements, combined with finite-element modeling of the multi-domain microstructure, we extract an effective piezoelectric coefficient d33eff of 53 pC/N, comparable to bulk BTO. Exploiting the intrinsic ferroelectricity, we further demonstrate low-voltage switching with a fast (100 ns) response, attractive for reconfigurable RF front-ends and parametric amplifiers. Extending these measurements to millikelvin temperatures, we find that the piezoelectric response persists, with d33eff 19 pC/N, pointing to the potential of BTO for piezoelectric coupling in superconducting quantum circuits. These results position thin-film BTO as a promising piezoelectric platform for both classical and quantum information technologies.
summary: This paper thoroughly characterizes thin-film Barium Titanate (BTO) resonators, demonstrating its strong piezoelectric response from room temperature down to cryogenic temperatures. By measuring SAW resonances and analyzing ferroelectric switching dynamics, the authors establish that BTO remains a viable, highly coupled platform for both classical RF electronics and emerging superconducting quantum circuits.
main_problem: The study characterizes the piezoelectric properties of thin-film Barium Titanate (BTO) across a wide temperature range, specifically investigating its potential for coupling in superconducting quantum circuits.
main_result: Thin-film BTO exhibits strong piezoelectric coupling ($d_{33,	ext{eff}} \approx 19 	ext{ pC/N}$ at millikelvin), which persists down to cryogenic temperatures, making it a promising platform for both classical RF and quantum information technologies.
method: The research combines microwave characterization of Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) resonators with finite-element modeling and scaling relations to extract effective piezoelectric coefficients across temperature regimes.
model_or_system: The physical system is an Interdigital Transducer (IDT) fabricated on thin-film BTO deposited on a Si substrate. The analysis models the material's ferroelectric, piezoelectric, and elastic responses under varying DC bias and cryogenic temperatures.
key_observables: Electromechanical coupling coefficient ($k_{2	ext{eff}}$), effective piezoelectric coefficients ($d_{31}, d_{33}, d_{15}$), resonance frequency shifts, and the temperature dependence of these parameters.
important_parameters: Temperature range (Room Temperature to millikelvin); high electromechanical coupling ($\sim 14\%$) and fast switching dynamics ($\sim 100 	ext{ ns}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on extracting coefficients via scaling relations at cryogenic temperatures due to measurement limitations, and assumes the persistence of piezoelectric coupling mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figures show SAW resonance spectra ($S_{11}$) at various temperatures, hysteresis loops ($\gamma_e$) demonstrating ferroelectric switching, and plots detailing the temperature dependence of coupling rates and coefficients.
paper_structure: The work progresses from characterizing room-temperature performance (high $k_{2	ext{eff}}$) to studying voltage-controlled reconfigurability, culminating in detailed measurements and analysis of piezoelectric response at millikelvin temperatures for quantum applications.
why_interesting: The demonstration that a classical ferroelectric material like BTO maintains significant coupling strength ($d_{33,	ext{eff}}$) down to the millikelvin regime is highly relevant for integrating solid-state transducers into superconducting quantum circuits and quantum memories.

FIG. 4. Temperature dependence of BTO’s piezoelectric response a, Measured S11 spectrum (blue) at 13 mK together with fitting (red dashed line) used to extract external coupling γe. Inset highlights one of the bulk acoustic modes (red arrow) with a fitted linewidth of 80 kHz. b, Hysteresis curve of γe at 13 mK up to 50 V, showing an increased coercive field and remanent polarization. c, External (γe, blue) and internal (γi, red) coupling rates as a function of temperature from 300 K to 0.7 K. Shaded color band marks the corresponding phase transition of BTO. The error bars in b and c are 95% CI from nonlinear fitting. The bias in a and c is 30 V.
